name: event-message
intent: Announce that something has happened by publishing an immutable, self-describing event message - a past fact that expects no reply - on a channel, so that any number of interested receivers can react without the producer knowing who they are or what they do.
problem: A component has completed a state change that other parts of the system care about, but it must not - and usually cannot - know which ones care. Calling each interested party directly couples the producer to every consumer, to their availability and to their processing order, and every new consumer (search index, audit, notification, analytics) forces a change and a redeploy in the producer. The trigger is open-ended interest: something changed, and the set of parties wanting to know is neither closed nor known at compile time.
context: Applies wherever a system reports occurrences instead of requesting work: integration between services over a broker or a log (Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, SNS/SQS/EventBridge), module boundaries inside one process (domain publishing to notification, search or reporting modules), and state propagation towards caches, read models or clients. It fits when the announcement matters more than any single response - audit trails, cache invalidation, read-model updates, downstream reactions - when consumers may be slow or temporarily offline, and when the producer's transaction boundary is the natural publication point.
benefits: Spatial decoupling: the producer knows only the channel and the event type, so new consumers subscribe later without touching or redeploying the producing system.
Temporal decoupling: publication is asynchronous, so consumers process at their own pace and a slow or unavailable consumer does not block the transaction that produced the event.
One-to-many fan-out: a single occurrence reaches any number of heterogeneous subscribers, each deciding independently what to do with it.
Availability: with a durable channel, the event survives consumer downtime and is delivered when the consumer returns; a broken consumer cannot fail the producer.
The event stream doubles as an audit log: each message records a fact with its timestamp, which observability, replay and event-sourcing consumers can reuse without extra instrumentation.
Consumers can be added for unplanned purposes (search index, compliance export, cache warming) after the fact, because the producer published facts rather than narrow commands.
tradeoffs: No reply path: an event is fire-and-forget, so a failed, ignored or unsubscribed event is invisible to the producer; the failure surfaces later as stuck downstream state.

The flow becomes implicit: a business process assembled from event notifications exists in no program text, so understanding, debugging and changing it requires tracing infrastructure (Fowler's event-notification trap).

Delivery semantics are weak: brokers deliver at-least-once, may reorder across partitions and drop events when retention or expiry passes, so every consumer must be idempotent, order-tolerant and able to detect gaps.

The event types are a public contract: renaming, moving or repurposing a type or payload field silently breaks consumers, so versioning, schema registry and tolerant readers become mandatory overhead.

Easy degradation into a passive-aggressive command: when the producer actually expects a specific reaction, styling the message as an event hides an intentional requirement and re-couples the systems invisibly.
Payload tension: thin events force every consumer to call back to the producer (extra load, temporal coupling), while fat events copy state, duplicate data and create stale replicas.
Operational and test cost rises: a broker in the loop multiplies environments, adds latency, and makes end-to-end tests slower and flakier than direct calls.

participants.responsibility: The immutable description of what happened: a stable type name, the facts of the occurrence and when it occurred; it carries no intent to invoke behaviour and is never modified after publication.
Detects the occurrence, creates the event, wraps it in the channel's envelope and publishes it once the state change is durable; it holds no references to receivers and expects no reply.
Carries the event from publisher to subscribers and decouples them in time and space; a publish-subscribe channel (topic, event stream, event emitter) when more than one receiver may be interested.
Retains events, tracks subscriptions and performs delivery (durability, redelivery, per-partition ordering, expiry); absent or replaced by an in-process dispatch list in process-local realizations.
Subscribes to the event types it cares about, decodes the payload and decides what to do; it sends no reply and must tolerate duplicates, reordering and unknown event types.

use_cases: Order placement in a service landscape: after the order transaction commits, OrderPlaced is published once and consumed independently by billing, warehouse, loyalty, search-index and notification services.
Cache and replica invalidation: CustomerAddressChanged tells every service holding a copy of the customer data to refresh or drop it, without the producing service knowing the replicas.
Audit and compliance: every state transition is emitted as an event to an append-only log, giving an ordered record of facts that a separate consumer turns into the audit trail.
Read-model / projection maintenance in CQRS: events from the write model update materialized views and search indexes asynchronously.

In-process module decoupling: a domain model publishes InvoiceIssued on an internal channel; e-mail, reporting and webhook modules subscribe without the domain importing them, keeping the dependency direction inward.
Platform-wide notifications: user lifecycle events (AccountCreated, PasswordResetRequested) fanned out to analytics, anti-fraud and e-mail consumers, each with its own retention and retry policy.

Financial trade confirmation: a matching engine emits TradeExecuted to a topic; clearing, risk management, position keeping and regulatory reporting services each consume the same event independently without the exchange knowing their identities or processing logic.

IoT telemetry ingestion: sensors publish DeviceReading events to a broker; stream-processing consumers compute rolling aggregates, rule engines evaluate thresholds, and archival systems persist the raw history — all decoupled from the sensor firmware.

Healthcare resource-change events: a FHIR-compliant system emits ObservationCreated, PatientUpdated and EncounterClosed events; downstream systems (clinical decision support, population health, billing) subscribe to precisely the event types they need without tight coupling to the EMR.

Apache Kafka event streams: producers append events (OrderPlaced, PaymentSettled) to a retained topic; consumer groups for billing, analytics and search indexing each read the same log at their own offsets, and a new consumer can replay from any point without the producer changing a line of code.

RabbitMQ fan-out notification: a producer publishes to a fanout exchange and the broker copies every event message to each bound queue - the official 'logs' tutorial has ephemeral subscribers joining and leaving while every bound consumer still receives every message.

GitHub webhooks: GitHub posts past-tense event messages (push, pull_request, release) with an event-type header, delivery GUID and HMAC signature to subscribed endpoints; integrations declare which event types they care about without ever modifying the producer.
avoid_when: The caller needs a result, an error or a guarantee that someone acted: use Request-Reply (or a direct method call) instead of hoping a consumer reacts.
A specific receiver must perform a specific action: use a Command Message, which states the intent explicitly instead of disguising it as an event.
The need is process-local and synchronous: plain Observer / callback registration or a direct call is simpler - no serialization, no broker, no eventual consistency.
A nightly batch pull already satisfies freshness requirements: an event stream adds infrastructure for a freshness nobody needs.
Several steps must happen in a fixed order with all-or-nothing semantics: an orchestrated command flow or Process Manager is easier to reason about than a chain of indirect events.
The message is fundamentally a data transfer whose content is the point: use a Document Message; if the producer already knows all the data, the timing of 'it happened' is decoration.
anti_patterns: Passive-aggressive command: publishing an 'event' when the producer actually expects a specific consumer to perform an action - the intent is hidden and the coupling smuggled back in.
Event as remote procedure call: DoSomething-style events with a reply channel and the producer blocking on the answer, which is Command Message plus Request-Reply wearing event clothing.
Chatty state dribbling: an event per field change carrying the whole aggregate, so consumers repeatedly rebuild state and replicas diverge.
Serialising internal domain objects or process state into the event payload, exposing the producer's model and freezing it into a public contract.
Fire-and-forget without discipline: no idempotency keys, no expiry, no dead-letter path, so duplicates, stale events and unprocessable messages accumulate silently.
design_principles: Loose coupling (Law of Demeter at system scale): the producer depends only on the channel and the event contract, never on concrete consumers.
Inversion of control: consumers register interest; the producer does not call them, so subscription is the subscriber's decision.
Open/closed principle: new consumers subscribe without modifying the producer or recompiling it.
Single responsibility: the producer announces, the channel transports, the consumer reacts - each party owns one concern.
Immutability and information hiding: an event is an immutable fact exposing only the data a receiver legitimately needs.
best_practices: Name events in the past tense and give each a stable, versioned type id (OrderPlaced, order.placed.v1) whose meaning is never reused for a different fact.
Publish only after the state change is durably committed (transactional outbox / after-commit hook) so no consumer ever sees a phantom event.
Keep payloads self-describing and minimal: identifiers plus the change facts; let consumers fetch details when they need them instead of shipping the whole aggregate.
Make every consumer idempotent and order-tolerant (at-least-once delivery, duplicates, reordering) and forward unprocessable events to a dead-letter channel.
Set an explicit retention/expiry per event type - a stale event is usually worse than a missing one - and never rely on guaranteed delivery for high-frequency notifications.
Manage event types like a public API: schema registry, contract tests, tolerant readers, deprecate-and-add instead of edit-in-place.
Instrument publication and consumption (counts, lag, dead letters) so the implicit business flow becomes observable.
Prefer a standard event envelope such as CNCF CloudEvents v1 (type, source, id, time, datacontenttype, data) to achieve vendor-neutral, schema-compatible events across cloud providers.

Use a transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business state change, then relay it asynchronously to the broker - this guarantees at-least-once delivery without two-phase commit on the broker.
Design consumers as stateless processors that checkpoint progress; do not store in-memory state that is lost on restart.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Messaging Solutions (2003) — Event Message (Message Construction, Chapter 3); 'use an Event Message for reliable, asynchronous event notification'.
https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/EventMessage.html — Pattern entry page with description and relationships.

https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/docs/EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns_HohpeWoolf_ch03.pdf — Chapter 3 'Message Construction' PDF covering Command, Document, Event and related message types.

https://martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html — Fowler, 'What do you mean by Event-Driven?' (2017); covers Event Notification, Event Carried State Transfer, Event Sourcing and CQRS with practical guidance and the event-notification trap.

https://cloudevents.io/ — CNCF CloudEvents v1.0 specification; graduated project providing a vendor-neutral, interoperable event format adopted by AWS EventBridge, Azure Event Grid, Google Cloud and many brokers.

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/sending-and-receiving-cloudevents-with-amazon-eventbridge/ — AWS Compute Blog: sending and receiving CloudEvents with EventBridge, idempotency, schema registry and input transformers.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/well-architected/service-guides/azure-event-grid — Azure Well-Architected Framework guide for Event Grid: event schema design, delivery reliability, dead-letter handling and schema governance.

https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/DocumentMessage.html — Document Message pattern (complementary; clarifies when to prefer a data-carrying Document Message over a lightweight Event Message).
https://ptgmedia.pearsoncmg.com/images/9780321200686/samplepages/0321200683.pdf — Sample pages from the EIP book (Pattern Overviews and Message Construction introduction).
https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/ — Apache Kafka official documentation: producers and consumers publish and subscribe to event streams on retained topics with consumer groups and replay.
https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/tutorial-three-java — RabbitMQ official Publish/Subscribe tutorial: a fanout exchange broadcasts every event message to all bound queues.
https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks — GitHub webhooks documentation: self-describing event messages with event-type header, delivery GUID and HMAC signature dispatched to subscribed endpoints.
https://berndruecker.io/how-to-tame-event-driven-microservices/ — Critique of event-driven microservices: the event-notification trap, hidden end-to-end flow and commands disguised as events.

https://www.nilus.be/blog/your_event_bus_creates_implicit_coupling/ — Critique: event buses create implicit coupling when consumers infer semantics from undocumented fields, ordering or omissions; generic events like CustomerUpdated collapse bounded contexts.
